P1.evidence: Genuine rapport before the frame — where he lives, where he is from, the two-week layover. The application was read and acknowledged: 'I did read through your application, so I kind of have a bit of a head start on where you're at, okay?' Agreement was sought and given. The open question was the scripted one, 'what could we potentially help you with today? Give me a rundown, I'd love to hear everything from you.' The frame was again three-part — 'where you're at, where you're trying to get to, what's kind of been getting in the way' — with 'what you need' missing, which is now consistent across every call by this rep in the batch.

P2.evidence: The most complete baseline in the batch. Age, height and weight taken; body fat and its source probed ('Is that like a Hume scale or which scale do you have?'); injuries asked and followed up ('But no pain associated with that at all?'); training week walked through in detail; a 1-10 satisfaction score on physique and the one thing he would change; diet walked through meal by meal; sleep, hours needed and daytime energy all covered; endurance and mobility asked as well, which the script does not require. P2b is partial because occupation was volunteered during the goals discussion rather than asked, though the sedentary follow-up was made. P2c is partial for hereditary conditions never being asked.

P3.evidence: Much the strongest goals work in the batch. 'What would be the main thing that you'd want to actually change with it?' produced the specific target; 'why the abs specifically?' produced the beach answer; the bridge ran cleanly; and the deep question was run properly — 'let's say we fast forward and we do get you to a point where... what does that actually do for you? What other areas of life would that really impact?' — which surfaced the San Francisco move, self-consciousness, and 'the type of person to like walk up to someone random and introduce themselves'. He then drove it to identity, career and future kids. P3c was never asked and P3h was a summary reflection rather than the 'this isn't really about the weight' move.

P4.evidence: Everything tried was surfaced — carnivore, near-zero-carb, meticulous calorie counting, YouTube dumbbell programmes, calisthenics, functional patterns — and each outcome came out. What did not happen is the root cause. The rep supplied the conclusion instead of extracting it: 'really what I'm hearing with all of this, we're just looking for the thing that can actually be sustainable', and got a one-word 'Yeah.' The prospect was never made to say why none of it stuck, and P4f was never run at all, which mattered later: the eventual objection was about deserving the purchase, and the root-cause work that would have exposed that was skipped.

P5.evidence: The two-year question ran and produced the best material of the call — 'it would just be like a mediocre lifestyle... the whole day is just kind of covered by this gray film over your eyes because you know you're not living the best life you could.' The rep then stopped working it. The settle question was asserted rather than asked — 'I kind of get the sense that's not something you're too willing to settle for. It could be wrong.' — and 'why not?' never followed, so the answer never had to be defended. Same pattern at the line in the sand: 'I kind of get the sense you're feeling like maybe it's time to actually draw a line in the sand.' Both got a yes; neither got conviction.

P6.evidence: Both questions ran and ran well, but out of sequence — the entire three-pillar presentation and the delivery walkthrough came first, so commitment was tested after value was pitched rather than before. The belief question was pressed properly: 'do you feel like ultimately, if we follow that, it can actually get you the results?' then 'Why do you feel that way, though?' which produced a detailed and genuine answer. The all-in question was asked verbatim in substance. P6c is the failure: real hesitation surfaced immediately — 'I'm making the calculations in my head about how big of an investment it would be and I'm not sure if I'm ready for it' — and the script says return to Phase 5. The rep instead pushed forward into price and closed for another half hour on a prospect who never gave a clear yes.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted — 'do you feel like, Hey, if we were able to do something like that, that this is something that you'd want to pull the trigger on right now?' — but no agreement was reached, so none of the payment or onboarding steps became reachable. Scored N/A rather than miss so an unsuccessful close is not double-counted against the rep.

objection_plays.detail: The burned-before trigger was explicit and named by the prospect: 'I think it's me feeling burned by the other... I just burned a whole bunch of cash for like, nothing. Like, and I just don't, it's a, it's like a terrible feeling.' The rep ran a competent improvised version — his own $200k of coaching spend, an honest split between what was his fault and what was a bad product, and the guarantee as the structural answer. What did not run: 'would it be fair to say you're looking for certainty?', the bridge and plane frames, the burned-in-a-relationship analogy, and 'how will you know if you never actually try?' The concern was isolated but never dissolved.

'I might have to just think about it a little longer' landed at 01:08:17. The rep correctly refused to accept it and re-ran the belief question, got a strong yes, and isolated: 'outside of the concern around like, what if I do this and I get burnt, like there's nothing else that's keeping us from being less than 100%?' He also ran a version of the identity move — 'that version of Roy, do you think it's a little bit easier for him to make money?' Missing were the central frames: 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?' The play was worked hard and never landed.

Isolation ran first, correctly. The financial picture was then only half taken: savings and checking were asked for directly — 'how much money do we actually have set aside right now, like, savings account checking?' — and deflected without a figure, and the monthly delta was asked and answered at roughly $1k surplus. Never asked: number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, crypto, stocks or investments. The 'should I versus how' reframe was not used. Most importantly the rep accepted 'we have the means to invest in this in cash' and did not press for the number, so the plan he improvised twenty minutes later was built on no figures at all.

A clear timing objection — 'it's mainly just like a timing thing', 'something that I can delay for two to three months'. The rep ran the spine of the play in his own words: he tested the premise twice ('what happens if it doesn't take off within a couple of months?', 'what happens if that one doesn't go through?') and told the regret story that carries 'the only thing you can control is right now'. He did not use the things-never-slow-down frame or ask when it actually becomes the right time, and he never got a commitment on what would have to be true in two months.

A partner-money dynamic was present and the rep himself put it into words — 'now I have to go to my partner, and he's really good with money, and I just be like, hey, I spent another X amount of dollars on it' — and the prospect confirmed 'I think so.' No part of OB was then run: no 'is there any reason he would not want you stronger', no responsibility frame, no deposit-and-go-talk-to-him option. The rep folded it back into the burned-before concern and it was never revisited, even though it resurfaced at the very end as 'my other obligations are also on my head.'

SCRIPT GAP — A WORTHINESS AND VALUES OBJECTION, NOT A MONEY ONE. The prospect could pay and said the outcome was worth $6,000, but would not buy: 'it's more of a principle thing and not, like, I would have the means to invest in the course, it's just, like, do I feel like I deserve this course, you know?' and 'I don't think it's fair to Trevor, like, given how much time he would have to spend.' He also operates a self-imposed rule that salaried 'difficult money' may not be spent on soft-return purchases. Nothing in the playbook addresses a prospect who can afford it and does not feel entitled to it. The rep improvised well — inverting the money rule so hard money exists to fund the path to not-hard money — and got agreement in principle without a decision. This is a genuine gap and, on an ICP of high earners, likely a recurring one.

SCRIPT GAP — A SECOND PERSON IN THE HOUSEHOLD. The prospect asked whether Trevor had ever coached two people who live together, on behalf of a partner with ankle issues who shares his training. There is no scripted answer. The rep gave the correct commercial one first — 'we'd be looking at two investments for the coaching program' — and then undercut it off-policy.

notes: Discovery, goals and consequence were the best in the batch and the emotional material the rep surfaced was excellent. Two coachable failures. First, a habit of asserting the conclusion and asking for confirmation — 'I kind of get the sense that's not something you're too willing to settle for' — which harvests agreement without conviction, and every one of those soft yeses collapsed at the close. Second, Phase 6: real hesitation surfaced at the commitment check and the script says go back to Phase 5. Instead the call ran another twenty-three minutes into price, then improvised a $1,200 trial and an unspecified instalment plan in the final two minutes against a disclosed hard stop. This deal was lost on structure, not on money — the prospect confirmed twice that he could pay cash.
